item.title: Evacuees of Ontario’s Wildfires Wait and Worry
item.description:
Scotty Frank rushed to the shore as a ferocious wildfire devoured his remote Indigenous community in northwestern Ontario. A friend who works for the railway had tipped him off to the fire’s path and Mr. Frank started knocking on doors. With little notice, all 26 residents climbed into fishing boats and chugged across the lake.

“Fire, angry fire, was coming right at us, and it was making its way along the shoreline,” said Mr. Frank, 29, of Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, whose arm hair was singed in the evening escape a week ago. “The heat, the smoke, it was terrifying seeing that behind us.”

On the water, the boats’ small motors churned against waves. The fire behind them thundered like a freight train.

“If we weren’t in our boats, we would have been stuck in that flame,” said Mr. Frank, who fled later that day for Thunder Bay, Ontario, a city of about 123,000 people 130 miles southeast of the fire region, that is hosting evacuees.

Wildfires tearing across northwestern Ontario have sent heavy smoke across major cities in Canada and the United States, displaced 1,800 people and fomented mistrust toward the provincial authorities, whom many evacuees blame for inadequate warnings about the danger.

Premier Doug Ford of Ontario, visiting Thunder Bay on Saturday, assured evacuees during a televised news conference that no expense would be spared for firefighting. Later that day, he stopped by an arena retrofitted to be an emergency shelter, with about 150 cots and supplies for evacuees still expected to arrive.

Some of the people who had been displaced to the city fumed.

“I am furiously angry,” said Joy Neill, the owner of Bear Paw Lodge, a fishing and hunting outfitter in Armstrong, Ontario, who evacuated to Thunder Bay. She learned that neighboring communities were leaving immediately from Facebook posts late in the evening on July 13. The police came knocking about 40 minutes later, Ms. Neill said, though she had already awakened her guests.

Exasperated residents fired questions at a worker from the province’s Ministry of Natural Resources, who presented maps and a wildfire update on Saturday afternoon in a Thunder Bay hotel conference room. According to the ministry’s data, the fire covered roughly 7.9 million acres — about half of the total area burned in the province.

“I have no understanding why the ministry was not on top of this weeks ago, a month ago even,” Ms. Neill told the room, her voice rising as she referred to sightings of fire in the area as early as May. Her neatly pinned hair shook slightly as she pointed a finger for emphasis. “This should never, ever have happened.”

The isolated region northwest of Thunder Bay where nearly 150 wildfires were burning on Monday is a destination for campers, some of whom relied on their survival skills, sleeping in canoes or paddling to sandbars in the lake to await rescue during the evacuations last week.

The constellation of lakes around Thunder Bay has been an advantage for firefighters, serving as both a buffer to flames and a water source for pumps and hose lines, said Dave Tarini, the city’s fire chief. But the lakes aren’t a sure defense.

“When those fires are very intense, there’s potential for it to jump across lakes, creeks, rivers,” Chief Tarini said. “We can’t always rely on them to provide a reliable natural boundary.”

Closer to the wildfires, a two-hour drive west of Thunder Bay, Quetico Provincial Park sits near the edge of the flames. On Sunday, the lake glistened and the wind was gentle under a beating sun. But new blazes had sprung up in the distance. The park was eerily empty, a hose running along the road every hundred feet or so to pump lake water into the sprinkler systems installed on camp cabins.

As nature offered no guarantees, residents rose to the challenges. Most firefighters in the sprawling region’s rural communities are unpaid volunteers, essential to the security of small-town living in northern Ontario.

At the Thunder Bay fairgrounds, volunteers tended to rescued livestock, and a hotel conference room became a donation hall. Boxes overflowed with teddy bears, and Crocs and boat shoes lined the floor. Tables were stacked high with donated clothing. Outside, an Indigenous healer offered herbs for lung health, like mullein and wintergreen, in small plastic bags.

Marilyn Matinet, a retired educational assistant from Whitesand First Nation, about 150 miles north of Thunder Bay, lingered in the donation hall, thinking of her pets. She evacuated in a frenzy last week. She managed to bring her dogs along, but her 11-year-old cat, Silver, hid despite the treats she left out to coax him. “I cried because I didn’t do his cat litter and I didn’t refill his water,” Ms. Matinet, 69, said. “I wasn’t thinking.”

Many of the 500 residents who fled Whitesand First Nation are homesick, a feeling that settled in about midway through the three-hour drive to the city.

“It was very emotional,” said Hope Tibishkogijig, a councilor with the first nation. “We didn’t know what we were leaving behind, if we were even going to have homes when we went back.”

A handful of residents, defying orders to stay away from the area, and returned to assist the ministry staff with building fire barriers around the community, which has so far been spared.

“Mother Nature — I don’t know, she’ll do what she has to do,” Ms. Tibishkogijig said. “But right now, she’s showing us mercy.”

item.title: Philippines Says Sailor Was Injured in Skirmish With Chinese Coast Guard
item.description:
The Philippine military accused China’s coast guard of injuring one of its sailors in a scuffle that broke out on Monday in the South China Sea, where the two countries have been locked in a decades-long territorial dispute.

The episode began when an inflatable Chinese coast guard boat approached the Sierra Madre, a beached World War II-era warship that the Philippines uses as a military outpost in a disputed reef, and lashed out at the Philippine sailors who approached in a boat to chase them away, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said in a statement.

The statement added that a Philippine sailor had been struck on the head with a wooden baton in the ensuing struggle, necessitating medical care.

The Philippines’ Department of National Defense decried the incident as another act of “harassment” by the Chinese coast guard that added to a “pattern of provocative and hostile behavior,” in a statement of Monday. “We simply cannot trust this belligerent neighbor.”

The Chinese coast guard has disputed that version of events, saying that the Philippine sailors rammed their patrol boat first before attacking its personnel with “oars, long sticks, and other tools.”

Accusing the Philippines of spreading propaganda, China’s foreign ministry said it had summoned the Philippine ambassador in Beijing over the incident, according to a statement published by state media on Tuesday. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines has done the same to China’s ambassador in Manila.

While several countries have longstanding territorial claims in the South China Sea, the dispute between China and the Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally, has been the most fraught.

Tensions in the region have steadily increased in recent years, with the Philippines denouncing the encroachment of Chinese vessels, which they say have used water cannons or lasers to harass Philippine sailors in the area. In another incident at the Second Thomas Shoal — where the Sierra Madre is beached — in 2024, a Filipino soldier lost a finger after a Chinese boat rammed his vessel.

The latest flare-up came just before the start of a series of high-level diplomatic meetings hosted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, where, among other agenda items like the wars in Myanmar and Iran, negotiations to ease tensions in the South China Sea are expected to continue. The gathering, which will conclude Thursday, is being attended by both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and China’s foreign minister, Wang Yi.

The Philippines, the current chair of the 11-member ASEAN, has made establishing a legally binding code of conduct to prevent escalations in the South China Sea a key priority for its tenure, which concludes at the end of this year. The code was proposed decades ago and Philippine officials have voiced optimism about recent progress. But intractable differences have loomed.

Chief among them is the landmark ruling by an international tribunal that dismissed most of China’s sweeping territorial claims in the South China Sea in 2016, including those on the area marked by the Sierra Madre. While there was no mechanism for enforcing the ruling, it was widely regarded as a major victory for the Philippines, which currently sees it as a legal base line for any maritime code of conduct. China, which refused to participate in the arbitration, has steadfastly rejected it.

The decision provided fodder for another dispute earlier this month, when, in response to the Philippines’ commemoration of its 10th anniversary, Chinese state media posted a video depicting the Philippines as a monkey doing the bidding of Japan and the United States.

While the United States does not have any territorial claims of its own in the South China Sea, it conducts regular joint military drills there with the Philippines, with which it has a mutual defense treaty. Beijing has denounced U.S. involvement as a major source of tensions in the region.

The U.S. State Department criticized what it called “dangerous and aggressive actions” by China in a statement on the incident on Monday.

In an opinion article published by Philippine media outlets ahead of the ASEAN meeting, Mr. Rubio reiterated U.S. support for the 2016 ruling, writing that “we will honor our obligations to the Philippines and other allies as they confront new and coercive threats to our shared interests.” But he stopped short of singling out China by name.

Jason Gutierrez contributed reporting from Manila. Ruoxin Zhang contributed research.

item.title: Lebanese Army Accuses Israeli Troops of Firing as Its Forces Deploy in ‘Pilot Zone’
item.description:
Israeli forces fired shots near Lebanese Army troops on Tuesday, both sides said, raising tensions as they took the first steps in a new U.S.-brokered plan to transfer control of occupied areas to Beirut after months of war.

There were no reported casualties in the gunfire, as Lebanese troops began deploying in a village in southern Lebanon after an Israeli withdrawal on Tuesday.

The incident occurred hours before President Joseph Aoun of Lebanon met with President Trump at the White House. The two leaders were expected to discuss the security situation in Lebanon, as well as efforts to secure Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory that it has occupied for months, since invading to battle Hezbollah.

The deployment was part of a phased arrangement under which Israel agreed to withdraw from areas in southern Lebanon while the Lebanese military moves in to secure them, allowing displaced residents to return. The areas, described as “pilot zones,” are meant to test a broader agreement reached last month between Lebanon and Israel to wind down the conflict.

The Lebanese Army said in a statement on Tuesday that it had begun deploying to the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiya in the southern Nabatieh district. The army urged residents not to return until the security situation had stabilized and asked them to follow the instructions of troops on the ground.

Hours later, the Lebanese military accused Israeli forces of opening fire near their units. In a statement, they added that “this act of aggression could hinder the implementation of deployment steps in the pilot areas.”

The Israeli military said in a statement that Lebanese forces entered an area outside of the designated “pilot zone.” Israeli soldiers “operating in the area fired warning shots into the air only, which did not endanger the Lebanese Armed Forces personnel, in order to distance them from the area.”

In Lebanon, critics of the deal say it has not set a firm timetable for Israel’s withdrawal, which is tied to the Lebanese government’s efforts to disarm Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group that the government does not control. Hezbollah was not party to the negotiations with Israel and has rejected the framework agreement.

Israel’s military said late on Monday that Israeli, American and Lebanese military teams were conducting joint planning and coordination to implement the agreement. As part of the deal reached last month, Israel and Lebanon also agreed to establish a military coordination group overseen by the United States.

The State Department said in a statement on Monday that the initial “pilot zone” operations would include the villages of Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiya. Israel and Lebanon have held rare diplomatic talks for months, meeting first in Washington and then in Rome.

Hezbollah has rejected the negotiations with Israel, as well as efforts by the Lebanese government to disarm the group, adding to uncertainty about the broader agreement, how it can be carried out and Lebanon’s fragile path toward stability.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday, Mr. Trump and Mr. Aoun said they would discuss ways to support the Lebanese Army and help stabilize Lebanon, which has faced severe political and economic crises in recent years. Asked whether he would speak to Hezbollah, Mr. Trump said he would, particularly if Mr. Aoun wanted him to.

“I would speak to Hezbollah,” he said. “I speak to everybody. I will speak to people that a lot of people think I shouldn’t be speaking to and things work out.”

On Tuesday, some analysts said that the Israeli withdrawal, though limited in scope, could offer the Lebanese government an opportunity to bolster its standing.

“Withdrawing from the area does not make a massive difference on the ground,” said David Wood, the senior Lebanon analyst at the International Crisis Group, a research organization. “But the Lebanese state will hope that it can use this first ‘pilot zone’ as a proof of concept, showing that the Lebanese Army can assert control effectively, and therefore the U.S. should push Israel to accept further ‘pilot zones’ in fully occupied areas of Lebanese territory.”

The latest round of fighting erupted in early March after Hezbollah attacked Israel in response to the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran that began in late February. More than 4,300 people have been killed in Lebanon and over 12,000 wounded in the latest conflict, according to Lebanese health officials. Israeli officials say at least four Israeli civilians and more than 30 soldiers have been killed.

By Tuesday afternoon, footage on social media and local television showed residents of the Zawtar al-Gharbiya, along with ambulances, attempting to access the area. But Abed Ezzedine, the village’s mayor, said that Lebanese troops had told residents they would not be able to access the town on Tuesday.

“The Lebanese Army is doing its best to clear the roads and streets within the town,” Mr. Ezzedine said in a phone interview. “I am anxiously waiting with other people to get into the town. I can’t wait to see Zawtar again.”

Hwaida Saad and Leo Sands contributed reporting.

item.title: Water Plants Under Fire in the Gulf Are Crucial to Civilians
item.description:
The resurgence in hostilities between the United States and Iran has put desalination plants under renewed threat across the Persian Gulf region, where tens of millions of people rely on such facilities for drinking water.

In recent days, Kuwait has accused Iran of striking energy and water plants, igniting fires that have forced officials to suspend operations at several facilities. Earlier in the war, officials in Bahrain and Iran said desalination plants in those countries had also come under fire.

Infrastructure that civilians rely on for survival is not generally considered a legitimate military target, and striking it could be considered a war crime. But the attacks on water resources are especially concerning in the Gulf region: Most nations there lack widespread access to fresh water and rely heavily on hundreds of desalination plants, complex operations where repairs can be difficult and time-consuming.

Desalination plants produce 90 percent of Kuwait’s drinking water, according to an analysis by the French Institute of International Relations. Oman (86 percent) and Saudi Arabia (70 percent) also rely heavily on the technology.

Such plants have proliferated in the region as climate change has made droughts more frequent and severe, and as desalination technology has improved. The plants either evaporate and condense salt water or filter it through fine membranes.

Iran does not lean as heavily on desalination plants as its neighbors, but has faced severe water shortages in recent years. Iran has accused U.S. strikes of disabling water infrastructure in locations including an island where officials say water access for 30 villages was affected. The Pentagon and Israel denied responsibility for those attacks.

Iran and the United States have accused each other of targeting sensitive infrastructure during the latest exchanges of attacks, and Iran has said it would respond to any U.S. attacks on its own infrastructure by hitting similar targets in nearby countries that are allied with the United States.

That has prompted calls from around the globe for vital infrastructure to be spared from attacks.

“As in any conflict, the protection of civilians and civilian objects is critical,” said Stéphane Dujarric, a spokesman for the United Nations secretary-general, speaking about the conflict in a briefing on Monday. “Vital infrastructure on which civilians rely for survival, including hospitals and water supplies, must be spared.”

item.title: What to Know About Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain
item.description:
President Trump on Tuesday reiterated his threat to bomb a suspected Iranian nuclear site known as Pickaxe Mountain, telling reporters that the United States would strike that area “pretty soon, and very heavily.”

“There’s not a thing they can do about it,” he said of the Iranians during an Oval Office meeting with President Joseph Aoun of Lebanon. “Normally I wouldn’t say that. If I thought they could do something about it, I would never say that.”

Little has been confirmed about Pickaxe Mountain beyond its existence. When Mr. Trump threatened to bomb the site earlier this month, he acknowledged that “we see no activity there” but that it was still a “possible target for a nice big fat shot right in their front door.”

Here’s what to know about Pickaxe Mountain.

Pickaxe Mountain is in central Iran, about one mile away from the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, which was bombed by the United States and Israel in March, during the current war, as well as during the June 2025 war. The mountain is known locally as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La.

According to the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, the mountain itself rises nearly 5,300 feet above sea level, and the facility is estimated to be buried more than 300 feet below it.

Experts say the site has been under construction since 2020 and is not yet operational. Satellite imagery shows that construction continued after the June 2025 bombings and that a security wall was recently built around the facility’s perimeter. Some entrances were also reinforced — possibly to protect against future attacks.

Iranian officials said in 2020 that Pickaxe Mountain would hold a plant to build centrifuges, after one at Natanz was destroyed earlier that year in what Iran deemed an act of Israeli sabotage. Centrifuges are machines that spin uranium at supersonic speeds to enrich it and produce nuclear fuel. The uranium would need to be enriched further, with many more steps taken, in order to build a nuclear weapon.

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful, but it has not allowed the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, to gain access to Pickaxe Mountain. Rafael Grossi, the director general of the I.A.E.A., told reporters early last year that he had repeatedly pressed Iran for more information about the site at Pickaxe Mountain but to no avail.

“We’re asking them, ‘What is this for?’” Mr. Grossi said. “They are telling us, ‘It’s none of your business.’”

The site at Pickaxe Mountain is buried so deep that experts say even the United States’ most powerful bunker-busting bombs, like the 30,000-pound bombs that blasted through Iran’s mountainside uranium enrichment facility at Fordo and disabled its centrifuges in June 2025, might not be effective.

The site at Pickaxe Mountain may still have weaknesses that could make it vulnerable to aerial attacks, but it “would be more suitable for ground forces to attack or sabotage,” the Institute for Science and International Security has said. Still, since the U.S. military would need to fly deep into central Iran to reach Pickaxe Mountain, troops could be left exposed to ground fire on their way in and to drone and missile attacks once on the ground.

item.title: A Wartime Rift in Ukraine
item.description:
For a while now, there has been a sense that the tide has turned for Ukraine in its war with Russia. Ukraine is attacking Moscow; it’s even getting praise from President Trump. So why did President Volodymyr Zelensky just fire his top general?

War can be uniquely challenging for democracies, where citizens expect to have a say and sometimes express their discontent on the streets. Today my colleague Andrew Kramer writes about the upheaval in Kyiv during what should be a moment of optimism. It’s a fight over drones, corruption, generational differences and more.

By Andrew E. Kramer

For a time, it looked like Ukraine was going to have a good summer.

After a winter of heavy Russian bombardment, the country was finding battlefield success, striking Moscow and hitting Russian ships in the Black and Azov Seas. It was finding diplomatic success, too, receiving billions of euros from the European Union and a promise from Trump that Ukraine could start manufacturing its own interceptor missiles. Ukraine was on a winning streak.

What snapped it was not a fearsome Russian offensive or another unraveling of relations with Trump. Instead, it was an outbreak of political infighting at home.

The defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, was openly clashing with Oleksandr Syrskyi, the country’s top general. Zelensky fired Fedorov last week, triggering major street protests. He then fired Syrskyi on Tuesday night.

(You can read more about the breaking story of the general’s dismissal here.)

The infighting has cracked the all-important sense of wartime unity and overshadowed the narrative that Ukraine is riding high in the war. Rather than capitalizing on its momentum, Ukraine is now grappling with military upheaval at a critical juncture — a reminder that being a democracy at war can be messy.

A generation gap

The rift has raised questions about how fully Ukraine, with its vaunted reputation for military innovation, is embracing the high-tech solutions that the popular, youthful Fedorov embodied.

During his tenure, Fedorov, 35, clashed with Ukraine’s generals, who saw aspects of his robot-war vision as fanciful and argued for the continued need for infantry deployments.

Fedorov was ultimately fired after he blocked purchases of artillery ammunition in favor of drones. Syrskyi insisted that the ammunition was still needed in the brutal trench fighting in the country’s east.

But Fedorov didn’t back down. Instead, he responded with a press conference, where he delivered the most scathing public critique of Ukraine’s military leadership so far during the war.

Fedorov accused the 60-year-old Syrskyi, an old-school general, of strategic shortsightedness — of thwarting the careers of promising junior commanders and resisting the drone and robot combat that’s transforming the war. He said he had sought to root out what he described as rampant corruption in defense procurement and made enemies as a result.

In the aftermath of his firing, protesters poured out into cities across the country, many of them carrying signs with variations on “Fedorov is innovation, old grandpas are degeneration.”

In the days since, however, what began as a show of support for Fedorov morphed into demands for Zelensky to fire Syrskyi.

Crowds in Kyiv, which included active-duty soldiers and veterans, began deriding the man who successfully commanded pivotal battles earlier in the war. Meanwhile, a cardboard cutout of Fedorov got cheers when it appeared on a balcony overlooking the demonstration.

Ukrainian leaders take street protests seriously. They’ve toppled multiple governments. They’re viewed as a pillar of democracy and as an important contrast to the authoritarianism of Russia under President Vladimir Putin.

It wasn’t long before Zelensky was holding back-to-back video calls with army commanders, showing a willingness to hear their complaints. By Tuesday evening, Syrskyi was gone.

When success breeds pushback

One Ukrainian journalist told me that the rift over how to wage the war had come into the open now “precisely because there are successes” on the battlefield.

The people advocating high-tech warfare felt vindicated and became more vocal, said Volodymyr Yermolenko, the editor of a culture and politics magazine. Then those favoring a more conventional approach pushed back.

But that sort of clash carries risks. “Ukrainian history shows that if we are united, it’s very difficult to win against Ukraine,” Yermolenko said.

“The biggest enemy is internal division,” he said. “Our history taught us this can be deadly.”

Will these firings be enough to restore unity?

A day after the police used tear gas and batons against young people protesting failures in the education system and a lack of jobs, thousands returned to the protest site in New Delhi.

Security forces had removed tents and parts of the main stage at the venue. But Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical movement that has become a vehicle for the frustrations of millions of young Indians — said that the protest would continue indefinitely. More than 40 percent of India’s population is under the age of 25.

It’s exceedingly rare for an entire family to successfully escape North Korea together. But one family of nine did just that, becoming among the few who have managed to defect since the country’s crushing pandemic lockdown.

To escape, they crossed a hill strewn with land mines to reach a secluded beach, where a small boat waited. To carry the two young children more easily, the family sealed them inside burlap sacks and hoisted them onto their shoulders. Once aboard, they headed out of North Korean waters. item.description:
Rain lashed a flimsy wooden boat as it tossed through a churning sea, its engine straining against the swell. Under the cover of a stormy night three years ago, the vessel was fleeing North Korea.

On board were nine people, including two small children and a woman who was six months pregnant. Only a couple of the passengers had seafaring experience. They eluded a patrol ship, speeding across the world’s most heavily guarded maritime border.

Soon after their boat lurched into South Korean waters, a high-speed warship of the South’s navy bore down on it, tearing the water in aggressive circles. Snipers on the vessel trained their laser sights on the chests of the three adult men on the wooden boat.

Through a loudspeaker, a voice boomed: “Are you lost? Engine trouble?”

The North Koreans shouted: “Please help. We are defecting.”

The red dots remained stubbornly fixed on their chests. The South Koreans were taking no chances: The three men were clad in North Korean military uniforms, camouflage for a high-stakes escape. Desperate, the men shouted into the boat’s cramped hold for the other passengers to emerge in order to prove that they were civilians. From below, the two children, a 5-year-old girl and 3-year-old boy, were hauled up first, both pale and wasted from seasickness. Only then did the red dots drop off.

The North Koreans, led by Kim Il-hyeok and his younger brother, Yi-hyeok, were bound together by blood and marriage. The brothers, both in their 30s at the time, were accompanied by their mother and their families: Il-heyok’s partner, who was pregnant, and Yi-hyeok’s wife, their two children, his mother-in-law and brother-in-law.

The family, who defected in 2023, were among the few who managed to escape North Korea after its leader, Kim Jong-un, imposed a crushing lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic. They arrived in their adopted country with rare insights into a nation that had been choked off from the outside world. Some details of their escape have not been previously reported.

“That night,” said Yi-hyeok’s wife, Yu-mi, “we crossed from a sea of darkness to a sea of freedom.”

Over several months of interviews in South Korea, Il-hyeok ​spoke with the same swagger that he had developed as a self-described “troublemaker” in North Korea. Yu-mi ​was reserved, pulling her legs tightly to her chest as she spoke. Her mother, who asked not to be named but agreed to be photographed, weighed every word, fearing how her comments might affect relatives left behind in the North. But they all spoke with conviction about why they had to leave North Korea. (The rest of the extended family declined to be interviewed.)

The brothers came from Pyoksong, a county in North Korea’s southwest.

During the famine of the late 1990s, their father, a railway security official, returned with grim accounts from the hardest-hit provinces: The emaciated bodies of children found outside train stations were frozen solid, thumping like frozen fish when they were tossed onto trucks headed to burial grounds. He was the first in the family to lose faith in a ruling class that was unable to feed its people.

One night after his sons reached adulthood, he took them to a hill and pointed toward a cluster of lights across the South Korean border.

“That’s where we should go,” he said. “To live and stand tall.”

Yu-mi lived in the ​nearby coastal town of Kangryong. From there, she could see planes glinting in the sun as they rose from Incheon International Airport, just across the water — a shimmering vision of possibility, yet unreachable for North Koreans barred from travel and cut off from the internet.

“Our country felt like a prison without bars,” she said.

Beginning in kindergarten, children sang the anthem “We Have Nothing to Envy,” even as they were mobilized to haul river water or scour hills for herbs and pine nuts.​ After long workdays, adults attended compulsory “life review sessions,” writing self-criticism and pledges of loyalty. When Kim Jong-un visited ​an island near Yu-mi’s town in 2013, soldiers and villagers swarmed into the sea in jubilation. She knew the scene was staged; ordinary residents, she said, had been banned from leaving home.

In the face of the propaganda, a contraband culture spread. South Korean films and dramas circulated on USB drives smuggled from China. In Kangryong, the devices also arrived inside plastic bottles released by South Korean activists across the water, along with rice and mini-Bibles. Officials warned the bottles contained poison, but South Korean entertainment was winning.

Il-hyeok idolized K-pop groups like Girls’ Generation and styled his hair in a mohawk like BigBang’s Taeyang. He was arrested for “capitalist delinquency” and released only after paying a bribe, his hair razored. He and his friends once secretly watched “Valkyrie,” the Tom Cruise film about the plot to kill Hitler. When the conspirators failed and were executed, his friends wept.

The brothers’ notion of deserting North Korea felt just as perilous. Their father forbade them from marrying, reasoning that the larger the family, the greater the risk of being caught while defecting. He then used connections to transfer Yi-hyeok, his youngest, to Kangryong, where he learned navigation, mapped guard posts, and cultivated ties with officials. Yi-hyeok became a helmet diver, who harvests seafood from the ocean floor, breathing fresh air piped through a surface hose. He eventually met Yu-mi.

Il-hyeok worked in North Korea’s shadow economy, bribing his way into opportunity and out of trouble. He butchered animals for restaurants, ran a small gold mine and bought rice stolen from state granaries, reselling it at a profit. He also grew disillusioned with the system he was gaming.

Then, in 2014, their father died unexpectedly. The South Korean dream seemed to die with him.

Where Il-hyeok, the older brother, was restless, Yi-hyeok was steady. He married Yu-mi in 2017, and the couple soon had their two children. He joined a military-run fisheries company, operating three vessels. Despite a United Nations ban, Chinese buyers worked openly in Kangryong, and on a good day Yi-hyeok could earn more than a typical worker​’s annual salary.

Il-hyeok began dating a kindergarten teacher. Defection was no longer a priority.

“When I mentioned it, my brother told me to watch my mouth,” Il-hyeok recalled.

The pandemic overturned everything.

North Korea imposed one of the world’s harshest lockdowns. In Kangryong, access to the sea was closed off with barbed wire and armed guards. Yi-hyeok’s boats rusted and his debts mounted. Officials claimed that South Korea was dumping infected bodies and waste into border waters. Yet boats supplying seafood to the top tiers of society continued to fish.

“The elites still ate whatever they wanted,” Yu-mi said.

Il-hyeok​ once filmed a gaunt toothless man in rags begging for food. The man said soldiers had shot a villager who tried to gather crabs.

“They are ruthless,” he said in a tired whisper. “Even if you won’t give alms, you shouldn’t break the beggar’s bowl.”

Public executions grew more frequent, targeting those accused of committing violent crimes like murder, which surged during the lockdown, or of distributing “nonsocialist” content such as South Korean dramas. Thousands, including the brothers, were forced to watch as rifle fire cracked across the execution grounds. The crowds dispersed in silence.

“The goal was to instill fear,” Il-hyeok said. “To erase any fantasy about the outside world.”

The authorities were closing in on him, too.

​He wanted to marry his girlfriend, the daughter of a farmer. In a system that claimed to be classless, marrying a woman who worked on a collective farm — even as a teacher — would mean a loss of status for Il-hyeok. Both families opposed the match. The couple moved in together anyway. Then, in 2022, Kim Jong‑un banned unmarried cohabitation. Offenders faced labor camps.

“I had to choose between her and North Korea,” Il-hyeok said. “I chose South Korea — and a true class revolution.”

The brothers no longer argued about whether to leave — only how.

By early 2023, North Korea had begun easing its pandemic restrictions. Yi-hyeok’s boats were among the first permitted back to sea. But the window to escape was already closing. The authorities were preparing to install surveillance cameras along the coast to deter defections.

The brothers spoke in code over the phone. “Good weather” meant a storm was coming, forcing patrol boats back to port. “We’ve got a good catch — come down here” meant Il-hyeok should bring their mother and his girlfriend to Kangryong.

The weather and the catch were ideal the night of May 6, 2023.

Yu-mi’s mot​her, a 52-year-old widow, signed up last, just five hours before departure.

“I could die trying to escape,” she said. “But if my family reached the South and I stayed behind, I’d be as good as dead anyway — the relative of traitors.”

Yi-hyeok’s brother-in-law, his fishing partner, slipped away by boat and waited offshore. The rest of the family crossed a coastal hill strewn with land mines to reach a secluded beach. To carry Yi-hyeok’s two young children more easily, the brothers sealed them inside burlap sacks and hoisted them onto their shoulders. Before they closed the sacks, Yu-mi caught her children looking up at her.

“I thought it might be the last time I’d ever see them,” she said. “I cried, and my husband teared up, too.”

Yi-hyeok’s brother-in-law spotted the prearranged signal — a flashlight blinking three times from the beach — and steered the boat in to pick up the rest of the extended family. Around 10 p.m., the 30-foot-long vessel pulled away, its engine throttled down to little more than a brisk walking pace as it tried to slip quietly toward Yeonpyeong Island in South Korea, just nine miles away.

Below deck, Yu-mi suddenly felt ​the engine roar to full throttle, filling the hold with black exhaust and leaving the women and children seasick. Her youngest child’s eyes rolled back. She carried him up for fresh air — and found the men on deck in a panic.

“That’s when I saw a searchlight from a North Korean patrol boat sweeping across the waves behind us,” she said. “My heart dropped.”

The brothers had already agreed on what to do if they couldn’t outrun a security vessel: strap life jackets and flashlights onto the women and children and send them into the sea, trusting the current to carry them south. The men would steer the boat away as a decoy, making a last stand with 20-inch knives and homemade red-pepper bombs. To lighten the boat, Il-hyeok threw anything heavy overboard — axes, wrenches, fishing net, his brother’s air compressor for helmet diving.

​He ran below deck, fastened a life jacket onto his partner and rushed back outside. She believed he was about to throw her into the sea to save the others. His mother​ thought her son had chosen to save his girlfriend before his mother.

“It gave me endless trouble with them, until I could convince them they’d misunderstood me,” he said.

Gradually, the searchlight behind them faded. The brothers later speculated that the fishing net they had thrown overboard had tangled in the pursuing boat’s propeller.

Their two-hour gamble ended shortly after midnight, after the South Korean vessel stopped them and all nine family members were brought aboard.

An officer greeted them: “Welcome to paradise.”

Before the​y disembarked, the officer raised his fist and shouted, “Fighting!” The English word — common in South Korea as encouragement — was unfamiliar to the North Koreans.

“But he was smiling and shaking our hands,” Yu-mi said, “so we assumed he wished us well.”

​In the South, Yu-mi studied to gain an accounting clerk certificate and found work at a school. Her brother enrolled in college, while Yi-hyeok returned to helmet-diving for seafood.

“My brother joked the diving gear here was so advanced he could fall asleep underwater if he wanted to,” Il-hyeok recalled.

Il-hyeok’s girlfriend gave birth to their first child in the South. The couple married in 2024 and soon welcomed another daughter. Il-hyeok is finding his footing in the South’s capitalist economy, trying part-time jobs at restaurants and operating forklifts and excavators.

The plunge into the South’s noisy democracy was overwhelming. Televisions offered endless channels — so different from the North, where only government broadcasts existed. Back home, Il-hyeok’s ​used motorbike was a prized status symbol​; now he found himself on highways crowded with modern cars. City squares rang with protests.

Yu-mi’s mother marveled at faucets that produced both hot and cold water. On her first day working at a nursing home, ​she faltered when colleagues asked for “napkins” — another English word she had never heard. The brothers’ mother was scandalized by a TV drama in which a wife slapped her husband. And when Il-hyeok first ventured beyond Seoul, the South’s capital, he dutifully called a police detective to ask for permission. The detective only laughed.

And then there were elections.

In the North, ​people lined up in formal dress to receive a ballot with only one name. ​They placed ​their vote in the “yes” box with both hands and bowed deeply to portraits of Kim Jong-un’s father and grandfather, who ruled before him. No one dared approach the “no” box.​ When Il-hyeok and his wife voted in June as South Korean citizens, they found voters arriving in shorts and slippers, earphones in place. The ballot was a bewildering list of names.

Yet, South Korea was no paradise.

After 19 months in the South, Yi-hyeok died in a diving accident in late 2024.​ The brothers’ mother and Il-hyeok’s wife were diagnosed with cancer.

Il-hyeok vented frustration at Seoul’s soaring housing prices. He is saving every penny to move his family out of their cramped, government-subsidized rental apartment. Still, he insisted the defection was “100 percent” the right choice.​ Before his death, Yi-hyeok appeared on television, explaining that he fled to spare his children the indoctrination of North Korean schools. His daughter is now a second grader at a South Korean school, and his son is in kindergarten. The children adapted fastest to their new lives, quickly embracing South Korean staples like fried chicken and pizza.

“My husband gave me and our children the freedom he promised before he died,” Yu-mi said.

The brothers also honored their father’s final wish: When their boat fled North Korea, they carried his ashes with them.

I’ve been captivated by the recent defection of nine North Koreans to South Korea. It is exceedingly rare for an entire extended family to escape together, especially across the heavily guarded maritime border dividing the two Koreas. As it turns out, their escape plan was actually years in the making. I’ve pieced their journey together — a tale of brutal hardships during the pandemic era and a daring search for freedom.

@Choe Sang-Hun This is a beautiful story -- of desperation, great courage, of the bitter-sweetness of "paradise." It also reminded me -- as it should all those who enjoy the luxury of freedom -- of my good fortune. Thanks for sharing this family's journey with NYT readers.

item.title: The Teenage Boys Digging for Their Mother’s Body
item.description:
He had hacked apart concrete and sawed through rebar and pressed on through heat and dust and exhaustion, persevering as men far bigger and stronger collapsed.

Now, on Day 25 of his search, Winder Delfín, age 17, had finally found what he was looking for. Deep in the tunnel he had dug with his brother Deivi, age 15, his father and his stepfather, Winder could make out the flower-print dress that belonged to his grandmother.

He hoped his mother and little brother were just beyond.

“There are bodies nearby,” he said, looking up at his father from the edge of the tunnel.

A month after a pair of history-making earthquakes ripped across Venezuela, the country’s hardest-hit state, La Guaira, remains a scene of grueling, painstaking searches for the dead. From dawn until far past dusk, thousands of survivors fan out across the remains of the residences that once stood just blocks from the beach, climbing onto the mountains of rubble with pickaxes and sledgehammers, fueled by an obsessive desire to recover the bodies of the people they loved.

Officially the death toll is 5,278, but the government has said it could be as high as 10,000.

The hands of the searchers bleed. Dust coats their lungs and reddens their eyes. At night, some sleep atop the debris, too tired to go anywhere else. They live on donated sandwiches and plastic thimbles of coffee and the hope that they can somehow heal through their efforts, that those taken so suddenly can rest once they are found.

The smallest are children or adolescents whose parents don’t have the strength to keep them away, or who have lost their parents altogether. Survivors call them moles because they can tunnel into tiny spaces, lighting the way with cellphones and headlamps and reporting back to the adults above.

In another place, this work might be done by professionals. But the Venezuelan state, its capacities debilitated by years of mismanagement, corruption and U.S. sanctions, has left the job of recovering bodies largely to civilian survivors and volunteers.

In La Guaira, soldiers are most visible marching back and forth along the streets, sometimes sweeping dust from the roads and lining up for food brought in by foreign aid groups.

Winder and his brother Deivi lived with their grandmother Carmen, 69, mother, Yusmani, 35, and brother Moissés, 10, in an apartment on the first floor of a 12-story public housing building. Yusmani had just begun a new job at nearby beach club, a vacation spot for wealthier Venezuelans.

On June 24, the day the quakes struck, the older boys had gone to play at a water park. On the way home, they said, the earth began to shake and they hugged each other and closed their eyes. When they opened them, their building was gone.

They spent that evening rescuing survivors, and have been digging through the rubble ever since. Their father, Deivid Delfín, 44, a barber, had been with their mother for 14 years. Their stepfather, Giovanni Berroterán, 50, had been with her for four. Now, the men were working together to find the woman they had both loved.

Mr. Delfín said that he knew the work was dangerous for his sons but that he did not know how to keep them away. He felt lost, he said, when they cried and ask him to explain what happened.

“I’m no longer a boy,” Deivi said one day.

It took them three weeks to hammer and drill through the 12 stories that had pancaked one on top of the other.

The boys, their fathers and two uncles had dug three different holes trying to locate Apartment 107. Their tools: a shovel, pickax, sledgehammer, jackhammer, saw, even a kitchen knife, all shared between neighbors.

With no women from the family around, the men often stopped to hug one another.

On Day 23, the adults critiqued Deivi’s use of the sledgehammer, telling him to swing lower to save his energy. Winder, slight for 17, wore a pair of child’s jeans, the words “Too Strong 4 You” etched on the fabric. His yellow work gloves, several sizes too big, made him look like Mickey Mouse.

On Day 24, Deivi opened a fourth hole and arrived at the living room. By evening, they were pulling out a pair of shorts belonging to Moissés, and a small white undershirt. Mr. Delfín, sitting at the edge of the hole in the twilight, held it to his cheek and cried.

On Day 25, a group of Christian volunteers arrived from the nearby city of Valencia, wearing shirts that said “love for your neighbor.”

Carlos Lizarraga, one of the volunteers, signaled toward the boys’ two fathers. “It happened to him,” he said, “but it could happen to me.”

Soldiers marched by with their brooms. A volunteer psychologist, Obtavio Guerra, stood at the edge of the collapsed building. He had counseled some 50 survivors in recent days, he explained.

“The emotional reality hasn’t surfaced yet,” he said, calling the search for the bodies a way for people to stay occupied, distracted. “It is lying dormant, like a wave that could arrive at any moment.”

From the hole that led to the boys’ living room someone pulled out their mother’s Bible. It was wet and twisted but intact, and Deivi opened it to the last pages, where she had made lists of favorite verses and ills she must have wanted to expel.

On one page she had started a grocery list: two plantains, two lemons. Out came another of her books, “What Young People Ask: Practical Answers.”

It was noon when they found the first body and Winder, lying on his belly in the hole, recognized his grandmother’s flower-print dress. For hours they tried to widen the tunnel so they could extract her. The men hacked at the concrete with hammers and picks; the boys hauled the chopped pieces out.

Above them, an excavator clawed at the side of the building.

The family pleaded with the operator not to disturb their work — they wanted to pull out the bodies themselves.

Finally, two volunteers put on white plastic suits, blue gloves and masks. Just one had a helmet. They descended into the hole, crawled into the tunnel, and placed Carmen’s body in a black bag.

More volunteers carried the bag down the mountain of rubble. The family huddled together. The boys stood in the crooks of their father’s arms and cried as one of the Christian rescuers said a prayer.

“Tomorrow we’ll be back,” said Mr. Lizarraga, “because there are two more bodies.”

A police truck pulled up and officers laid Carmen’s body in its bed. Their father and stepfather climbed in, too, headed off to identify the body.

It took another 24 hours to locate Yusmani and Moissés, who had been in the kitchen. Mr. Delfín fainted before they were pulled out and had to step aside. But Winder kept working late into the night, unfurling a body bag for his mother and freeing her from the place she had died.

item.title: France Joins a Global Move Toward Restricting Social Media for Children
item.description:
France passed a landmark law on Tuesday restricting access to social media for anyone under 15, the first European country to do so, and the latest in a wave of countries acting against what they view as malign effects of such services on minors.

The law, approved by wide margins in both houses of France’s Parliament, could go into effect as soon as Sept. 1. It will also ban the use of cellphones in high schools, extending a prohibition that already applies to primary and middle schools.

A personal priority of President Emmanuel Macron, the law is viewed as a bellwether for other European countries, several of which are drafting their own laws. The measures come in response to concerns over online bullying and coercion, exposure to extreme content, the threat of predators and potential harm to mental health.

And yet it was on social media that Mr. Macron hailed the news. “I had promised it, and now it has been voted on: Social media will be banned for those under 15 starting back-to-school,” the president posted immediately after the National Assembly voted.

Last December, Australia became the world’s first country to bar anyone under 16 from using many social media apps. Britain and Canada moved toward similar measures last month, while Italy, Poland, Portugal, Spain have all drafted laws. The European Union is expected to introduce E.U.-wide measures in September.

But early evidence suggests that Australia’s ban has largely failed to keep young teenagers off social media. And enforcement of the French ban would likely fall to the European Union rather than the French government, which has limited legal tools to target major international internet platforms.

Social media companies have criticized age-related bans, saying they already employ safeguards to protect young users. Elon Musk, the owner of X, has called these laws a “backdoor way” to control access to the internet.

“France wants to push its own legislation to make the E.U. act, and the E.U. act fast,” said Jessica Galissaire, a senior policy researcher at Interface, a think tank based in Berlin. “I see it more as a political announcement.”

For Mr. Macron, who is term-limited and will step down in May 2027, it will likely be one of the last legislative milestones of his decade in office.

“It is clear that before the age of 15 or 16, social media is not a good thing,” Mr. Macron said last year. “This is because at that age, we have not yet sufficiently consolidated things on an affective, emotional and cognitive level.”

The president drew an analogy with laws restricting the consumption of alcohol by young people, which he said had changed behavior. “Sixty years ago, kids were served wine,” he said. “There may still be people who serve beer to infants, but in my opinion, they are not in a majority in the country today.”

France has staked out a strong position on reclaiming what officials call “technological sovereignty” from the United States and China, announcing plans to replace Zoom and other American software with French-developed alternatives. The new law can be seen within that context, Ms. Galissaire said, noting that, in France, the most popular social media platforms remained American and Chinese.

While the law passed comfortably, it drew opposition from some on the left, who say it does not adequately distinguish the services that must apply age verification. Lawmakers from France Unbowed, a far-left party, said they would vote against it because it threatened the principle of anonymity online.

Lawmakers from the Senate and National Assembly held prolonged negotiations on the law’s wording, mostly to bring it into compliance with European Union requirements. The European Union offered guidance on an earlier draft, which resulted in several provisions being stripped out.

Under the terms of the law, it would be up to social media platforms to use age verification systems to filter out underage users. There are exceptions that would allow young people to access online encyclopedias or other digital services with an educational purpose. The law does not provide for penalties against children or parents. Nor does it set out explicit penalties against the providers.

Most of the services targeted by the law are not based in France, which means the primary enforcement would fall to the main E.U. executive body, the European Commission, or to the countries where the companies are based. The E.U. would act through the Digital Safety Act, which seeks to protect children from harmful effects of social media.

The European Union recently received an expert report recommending that children under the age of 13 not have access to social media sites, unless they were supervised. The report recommended that 13- to 18-year-olds should only have access to platforms with safety features like limits on infinite scrolling. Children under the age of 3, it said, should have no screen time at all.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is expected to introduce new measures in September. But it could take a year or two for them to be implemented, Ms. Galissaire said, which helped explain France’s urgency.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: Houthis in Yemen Edge Closer to Entering U.S.-Iran War
item.description:
As the U.S. war with Iran spilled across the Middle East over the past five months, Yemen largely stayed on the sidelines.

That was until Monday, when the Iranian-backed Houthi militia, which controls a significant part of Yemen, declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally. The move threatened to open a new front in the regional war and further disrupt global energy supplies.

Here’s what to know about the rising tensions in Yemen.

Sources: Area of control via the Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute.

Lazaro Gamio/The New York Times

The Houthis, a rebel group from Yemen’s northern highlands, seized control of the capital, Sanaa, more than a decade ago with the help of Iran. Saudi Arabia, which borders Yemen to the north, then led a failed military intervention in 2015 to oust the Houthis and restore the internationally recognized government. The intervention set off a devastating civil war that dragged on for years.

The war largely settled into a fragile stalemate since a cease-fire in 2022. But last week, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking Yemen’s main international airport in Sanaa in a dispute over an Iranian plane that tried to land there.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government claimed responsibility for the attack. However, the Yemeni government does not have a functional air force and relies heavily on military support from Saudi Arabia.

The sudden rise in tensions raised questions of whether the Houthis would enter a war that, for the most part, they have stayed out of until now.

Analysts say Iran may be urging the Houthis to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea, which would cause further upheaval in the global energy markets. Oil prices have shot up in the past months as a result of dueling Iranian and American blockades of the Strait of Hormuz, another critical waterway for global shipping and energy supplies.

With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed for months, the Red Sea has become a vital alternative export route for the transportation of Saudi oil and gas.

In early July, a Houthi delegation attended the funeral in Tehran for Iran’s slain supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening salvos of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. When the Houthi delegation returned, Yemen’s government tried to block their Iranian flight from landing in Sanaa, prompting the Houthis to accuse Saudi Arabia of bombing the runway.

One senior Yemeni official said that they believed the plane was “carrying personnel and military dual-use equipment” from Iran.

The Houthis retaliated by attacking the Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia, the first direct Houthi strike on Saudi soil since early 2022.

Days before the Houthis announced a naval blockade on Saudi ships, their leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, warned that all Saudi ⁠oil and energy facilities would become targets if the kingdom escalated militarily.

Iran sees the Houthi threat to the Red Sea as potential leverage in its war with the United States, said Ahmed Nagi, a Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group. The group controls the part of Yemen that hugs the Bab al-Mandab, a narrow strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

“I think the message from Iran is: Don’t assume our leverage is limited to the Strait of Hormuz. We also have an ally that can threaten the Bab al-Mandab if needed,” he said.

The Saudi-led coalition will respond to all Houthi threats against transiting vessels “swiftly and firmly,” Turki al-Malki, the coalition spokesman, said in a statement posted on social media on Monday.

Late on Monday, Yemen’s defense minister, Taher al-Aqili, said the army of the internationally recognized Yemeni government would be ready “to end the Houthi coup.” Rashad al-Alimi, Yemen’s exiled president, called on people living in Houthi-controlled areas to “align themselves around the state.”

The Houthis did not give any specifics about how they would enforce a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia. But they have used their ability to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea as a weapon before.

During the two-year war in Gaza which began in late 2023, they attacked commercial shipping there with drones, missiles and hijacking, attempting to exert pressure on Israel and its allies.

They could use the Red Sea again to exert pressure on Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has relied on Red Sea routes in recent months to export more than 3.6 million barrels of oil and related fuels a day, most of it to Asia, according to the maritime data firm Kpler.

Yasir al-Rumayyan, the chairman of Saudi Arabia’s state oil giant, recently said the ability to bypass the blocked Strait of Hormuz and use Red Sea export terminals had been a “lifeline” for the kingdom’s economy.

A Houthi blockade could affect more than 3 percent of the global oil market.

“The Red Sea is always an easy way in which they can make the world bleed,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House.

“The Houthis are banking on insurance costs going up and panic among the global shipping industry like what happened during the war in Gaza.”

item.title: Trump Is Squeezing Canada. Don’t Expect Carney to Roll Over.
item.description:
For Canada and the United States, it was always going to be a bumpy summer.

Ever since the United States on July 1 declined to renew the trade deal President Trump negotiated with Canada and Mexico in his first term, the Canadian government, and many Canadians, have been bracing for his administration to try to use pressure tactics to extract concessions on trade.

On Monday the administration did just that, upping the ante, as Mr. Trump made use, for the first time in history, of a nearly century-old provision to impose fresh tariffs on the second-largest U.S. trading partner.

But the move is more likely to elicit stoicism than panic from the Canadian side.

The tariffs, which experts expect to face legal challenges, target more than 500 Canadian goods, including cheese and hockey sticks, worth $20 billion. That’s about 2 percent of the entire trading relationship in goods between the two neighbors, which was worth some $720 billion last year.

Those goods are virtually all covered by the upended United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a free-trade pact known as the U.S.M.C.A. In 2020 it replaced and updated the North American Free Trade Agreement, which took effect in 1994.

Mr. Trump, who negotiated the U.S.M.C.A. during his first term, at the time called it the “largest, fairest, most balanced and modern trade agreement ever achieved,” but has criticized it in his second term as the worst agreement ever. That deal, and the 1994 one, known as NAFTA, between them have for decades shaped the economy of the United States and its North American neighbors, Canada and Mexico.

Mr. Trump and the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said on Monday that the new tariffs were intended to punish what they labeled Canada’s “discriminatory” treatment of the U.S. auto, dairy and alcohol industries. In introducing the tariffs, Mr. Trump raised his often-repeated narrative that Canada is a mooch on the United States.

In a statement accompanying the new measures, Mr. Greer highlighted his disapproval of the fact that Canada had taken retaliatory tariffs against some U.S. goods in response to American levies, the only country to do so other than China.

The response by Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada was dispassionate.

“This is the latest in a series of unilateral U.S. trade actions that began with the U.S. imposing a series of tariffs” violating the U.S.M.C.A., Mr. Carney said in a statement on Monday. “Canada, as is its right, has merely matched those measures,” he added.

The new tariffs came days after Mr. Trump threatened Canada with sanctions for the wildfire smoke that has drifted from the blazes raging in Ontario to U.S. cities.

Mr. Carney was elected last year on a wave of profound concern and anger at Mr. Trump’s belligerent rhetoric toward Canada. He promised to build a sustainable trade agreement with Mr. Trump but also make Canada more independent of the United States.

He has pledged to double trade with non-U.S. economies by 2035, and has relentlessly traveled the world seeking investments and new trading partners. He has turned to both Asia and Europe to strengthen Canada’s economic and strategic alliances, and has made it plain that diversification away from the United States is his core U.S. policy. He has even suggested that a Canada with stronger global ties is a better partner to the United States.

The Canadian economy has treaded water through all of this and so far avoided a meaningful recession. But U.S. tariffs on goods such as steel, aluminum and vehicles have hit sensitive sectors, and the broader uncertainty around Canada’s relationship with its top partner affects the investment environment, which values stability.

The Canadian public seems to support Mr. Carney’s approach, handing him persistently high approval ratings in polls. Sentiment about the United States seems to have suffered more. Significantly fewer Canadians have been traveling to the United States for tourism over the last year according to Canada’s national statistics agency. And a recent Pew poll showed that only 35 percent of those surveyed in Canada describe the United States as a reliable partner, down from 83 percent in 2022.

New data released on Tuesday by Abacus, a Canadian opinion research company, shows Mr. Carney has broad backing to resist Mr. Trump’s escalating pressure to settle for a less advantageous trade agreement.

While six in ten Canadians polled believe reaching a deal with the United States over trade is urgent, only one in five said Canada should “be willing to make compromises to reach an agreement sooner.”

“Prime Minister Carney has a lot of room to maneuver in negotiations with the Trump Administration,” said David Coletto, who leads Abacus. “Over the past year, Canadians have gone from being overly anxious about how tariffs might impact their lives and wanting a speedy resolution, to now feeling that a bad deal that rewards troubling behavior is a non-starter,” he added.

These data points suggest that Mr. Carney has support at home to play hardball. Canadians generally want him to strike a fair and lasting deal, unlike many of the United States’ other trade agreements, which have been seen as fickle.

That grace is most likely not infinite. The opposition Conservative Party continues to strongly criticize Mr. Carney for failing to strike a deal with the United States, calling on him to take action to salvage the relationship and decrying some of his overseas outreach as theater rather than substance.

“President Trump is wrong to target Canadian workers and must reverse these tariffs immediately,” Pierre Poilievre, the Conservative leader, said in a statement on Monday, adding, “And Mark Carney was wrong to surrender Canada’s leverage for over a year and a half, without actually working to secure the deal he promised.”

Many Canadians remain worried about the impact that an aggressive United States can have on their lives, particularly the possibility of permanently tearing up the U.S.M.C.A. rather than just declining to renew it, which will lead to more negotiations.

Still, Mr. Carney is likely to hold out in protracted talks this summer, rather than roll over. At the very least he has until Aug. 19, when Mr. Trump’s newly announced tariffs are set to take effect.

In his statement on Monday evening, Mr. Carney reminded Canadians that this battle was about more than the economy, invoking Mr. Trump’s “threats to Canadian sovereignty,” a reference to the president’s repeated claims since late 2024 that Canada should become the 51st American state. That quip animated many Canadian voters to elect Mr. Carney last year.

Mr. Coletto said that Mr. Carney’s optimistic alternative, which includes deeper engagement with other parts of the world, is giving Canadians hope despite the dire situation with the United States.

“There’s an optimism and a new resolve that Canada ‘has what the world wants’ and, even if there is pain in the short term, uncoupling our relationship with the United States will be good for us in the long run,” he said.

item.title: Netanyahu Ad Uses a Questionable Tactic Against Bereaved Rival
item.description:
At first glance, it was the latest in a long line of anti-Arab campaign ads from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel.

An A.I.-generated video that Mr. Netanyahu posted Monday night showed his leading rival in the upcoming election, Gadi Eisenkot, rushing through an idyllic meadow past the outstretched arms of a young man wearing a T-shirt saying “Israeli unity,” to instead embrace Mansour Abbas, the Arab-Israeli lawmaker who heads an Islamic party.

The point, which Mr. Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party have driven home in at least a dozen other ads since June as Mr. Eisenkot has surged in the polls, was visceral and obvious.

It is aimed at Jewish voters who — whether traumatized by the 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, concerned about national security, or just plain racist — cannot abide the thought of their next government relying even partly on the support of an Arab political party to form a ruling coalition.

But this ad was different in one crucial way.

The young man in the video who reaches out in vain to embrace Mr. Eisenkot bears a striking resemblance to the candidate’s 25-year-old son, Gal, who was killed in the recent Gaza war. He died in a tunnel explosion in Gaza in December 2023 while serving as a reservist in an army commando unit.

Which lends an entirely different meaning to the expression on the face of the A.I.-generated Eisenkot, and to the Elysian field that provides the ad’s setting.

Before he retired from the military and entered politics, Mr. Eisenkot, 66, was Israel’s highest-ranking general, the chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, and an enormously popular one at that. Thousands attended his son’s funeral, including Mr. Netanyahu, and countless more watched on television as Mr. Eisenkot broke down repeatedly in delivering the eulogy.

The ad drew widespread expressions of disgust and outrage on Tuesday, including from several bereaved relatives of others killed in the Gaza war — so much so that by day’s end on Tuesday, Mr. Netanyahu’s team had issued a new version of the ad that removed a key element.

Among the critics was Gil Dickmann, whose grandmother was killed on Oct. 7, the day of the Hamas-led attack on Israel, and whose cousin was taken captive and later killed in Gaza.

Mr. Dickmann called it appalling and unbelievable that Mr. Netanyahu, who he said “was in charge on Oct. 7 and in all this failed war, allows himself to mock in this despicable way a mourning father like Gadi Eisenkot.”

And Einav Zangauker, whose son Matan spent two years held hostage in Gaza, assailed what she called the prime minister’s “incitement machine.”

“When the video started playing and I saw Gadi running with open arms, the thought crossed my mind that, from the other side, we’d see his late son Gal running into his father’s arms,” Ms. Zangauker wrote on X. “A hug like that would have warmed the heart. But what was I thinking? This is Netanyahu.”

Ms. Zangauker was a Netanyahu voter, she said, until the war turned her against him.

Mr. Eisenkot, whose party is running neck and neck with Mr. Netanyahu’s ahead of the Oct. 27 election and is ahead in some polls, declined to comment. But others in his Yashar party (Hebrew for “straight” or “honest”) spoke out.

“There’s no bottom to the pit the Likud is willing to sink into,” Matan Kahana, a right-wing former lawmaker running on Mr. Eisenkot’s slate, said in a radio interview.

A spokesman for Likud, Gil Levi, denied that the young man in the ad resembled Mr. Eisenkot’s son or that the ad was intended to invoke him in any way. He said that left-wing opponents of Mr. Netanyahu had invented this “to distract from the message of the ad — that Gadi Eisenkot is going to build a government with terror supporters.”

Demonizing Arab parties is a longtime Netanyahu strategy that exploits the fact that the centrist and left-wing parties often fall short of winning a majority in Parliament without the support of Arab factions, whose constituents make up roughly a fifth of the population.

But the criticism was not confined to the political left.

Limor Livnat, who was once the highest-ranking woman in Likud before quitting the party in 2021, scolded the prime minister for running “a video like that on a rival whose son fell in the war you managed and failed at.”

Mr. Dickmann, 34, of Tel Aviv, who is studying psychology, said he believed that the new Netanyahu ad was working exactly as it was intended.

“They’re trying to make you think, ‘Did they mean it or not?’ And to make us talk about it, so it goes viral,” he said. “But I can’t believe that no one around Netanyahu was able to say, ‘Do you think it might resemble the son?’ And if they didn’t, that means they’re so disconnected from reality that he’s even more dangerous.”

Mr. Netanyahu has been accused before of crossing lines of political propriety.

In 2019, he apologized for and pulled from circulation a campaign ad that briefly used the graves of Israeli soldiers killed in battle as a backdrop.

On Tuesday, he did neither, but he did show that he had registered the criticism.

Decrying what he called a “shocking attempt by extremists online” to misconstrue his earlier video, he released a new version of the ad. It shows a young woman wearing the “Israeli unity” T-shirt and looking forlorn as Mr. Eisenkot spurns her embrace.

item.title: India’s Young Protesters Are Bloodied but Unbowed
item.description:
They flocked to New Delhi by the thousands. Young Indians demanding accountability from their government for a flawed education system, hoping for a promise or a signal from those in power that would reassure them about their futures.

Instead, the throng of protesters who tried to march to Parliament on Monday were confronted by security forces, batons in hand, tear gas canisters ready. As the crowd swelled, the police cracked down, striking people’s shins, calves and backs, swinging their staves overheard. Protesters hurled flip flops and water bottles back. Many rushed to escape through back alleys and side roads. Plumes of tear gas left people choking.

The protesters — mostly young people who chanted slogans, carried posters or stood quietly in solidarity — said they were shocked by the police crackdown and the lack of any real government response. By Tuesday, their sense of anger remained palpable as thousands returned to the protest site near Jantar Mantar, an 18th century observatory, undeterred by spurts of monsoon rain.

Security forces had removed tents and parts of the main stage at the venue. But Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical movement that has become a vehicle for the frustrations of millions of young Indians — said that the protest will continue indefinitely. He implored people to keep it peaceful.

Leaders of the C.J.P. said 150 protesters were taken to the hospital from injuries in the protest on Monday. The Delhi Police said 118 of its officers were injured during “violent protests.” Around 70 protesters were detained, according to lawyers’ groups.

Although Prime Minister Narendra Modi has not responded publicly to the protests, on Tuesday he spoke through an emissary. Kiren Rijiju, the parliamentary affairs minister, told reporters, “The safety, security and future of our youth are our priority.”

He also provided assurances that future paper leaks would be prevented.

Mr. Modi rarely responds to critics, so the comments appear to be a sign of the importance the leader has placed on the youth protests and a tacit acknowledgment of the political risk of alienating young voters in a country where more than 40 percent of the population is under the age of 25.

However, the government has said little in response to the specific demands of the C.J.P., which include the resignation of India’s education minister, whom the C.J.P. holds directly accountable for a shoddy education system and leaks in recent entrance exam papers that forced millions of students to retake their tests.

“The government is in no mood to understand us and talk to us,” Chandan Mandal, a 19-year-old high school senior from the state of Rajasthan, said on Tuesday. He said he first protested more than a month ago. According to the C.J.P., at least 21 students have died by suicide since the exam leak, unable to handle the stress.

The police struck him with a baton three times on Monday, Mr. Mandal said. Two reddish bruises, each about three inches long, and an open wound were visible on his back.

“I’m opposing the government itself now,” said Mr. Mandal, who is studying for an entrance exam for engineering school.

A big reason for the frustration millions of young Indians feel is that there aren’t enough jobs, or that there is a mismatch between available jobs and qualifications, according to economists. A recent, widely cited study from Azim Premji University found that 40 percent of young people under 25 are unemployed, even as access to higher education has increased.

The protesters’ most visible slogans as they gathered on Monday morning were less concerned with botched exams than with the government’s overall accountability.

“India is a Democracy! We Need Answers!” read one, in English. “In Search of the Misguided,” read another, in Hindi, next to a hand-drawn sketch of Mr. Modi.

By the afternoon, the police waded in. Cries of pain rose above the shrill police whistles and sirens of riot control vans. A thin, young woman crouched on a median, as her friends dressed a fresh wound on her forearm and rinsed her face, reddened by tear gas.

At the Janpath subway station nearby, a police van lay overturned on its side, its windshield smashed.

Further away from the violence, Wishwas Srivastav, 36, an engine builder, said he had traveled to Delhi from the state of Himachal Pradesh to join the protests.

“It hasn’t been feeling like democracy here for the past 10 or 15 years,” said Mr. Srivastav. Of the government, he said, “I hope they’re listening.”

By Tuesday morning, traffic along Janpath was back to normal, with some of the cross-streets more tightly barricaded. The police van at the metro station had been flipped upright.

At the protest site, volunteers distributed food and drinks to protesters, including burgers from McDonald’s, samosas, water and electrolytes.

Abhishek Kumar, 20, sat in the shade, tired after a roughly eight-hour bus ride from his hometown of Kanpur. After watching the protests on social media on Monday and seeing the police beat protesters, he said, he decided to join in person. Mr. Kumar, who recently took an entrance exam to join the armed forces, said he would stay for a few days.

Many who gathered were parents worried about the future their children stand to inherit. Mina Ganesh, 51, was at the protest site on Tuesday with her son Miher, 17.

“Finally someone in the country is willing to speak up,” Ms. Ganesh said. “It took us long enough. Now that we have begun to speak up, there’s no stopping us.”

Miher, who wants to study either economics or engineering, said he was moved by the actions of Sonam Wangchuk, a prominent education activist who has backed the C.J.P.’s demands and joined its protest with a hunger strike.

Mr. Wangchuk is now 23 days into his fast and was forcibly moved to a hospital on Saturday by the government.

“He doesn’t know any of us,” Miher said. “How can I sit at home knowing he’ll die for me?”
