item.title: 3 Arguments Fueling Anti-Immigrant Sentiment in South Africa
item.description:
Foreigners have been forced out of their homes and businesses. Some have been physically attacked. Tens of thousands have fled the country.

Anti-immigrant sentiment is spreading in South Africa, driven by accusations that have become familiar across the world — that foreigners are committing crime, taking jobs and using valuable public resources.

South Africa is the largest economy in Africa, attracting many migrants from neighboring countries. There are about three million documented immigrants living in the country, and many more who are undocumented.

But are the accusations against immigrants in South Africa true? Here is what data and research say about three common arguments used against them.

South Africa reports one of the world’s highest murder rates. But police statistics show that immigrants are arrested at low rates.

While foreign nationals are about 5 percent of the population, they accounted for just 3 percent of arrests over the past five years, according to South African police data that was provided to The New York Times in response to a public records request. They accounted for just 1.2 percent of arrests for violent crime.

The data shows that nearly one in five arrests of foreigners is for immigration violations. At the same time, other statistics show that foreigners occupy South African prisons at a disproportionately high rate.

Last year, South Africa’s corrections department reported that more than 12 percent of inmates serving sentences in the country’s prisons were foreigners.

South Africa’s unemployment rate has hovered over 30 percent for the past several years, and many South Africans say that they haven’t reaped the benefits of living in Africa’s most developed economy.

The sight of foreigners waiting tables at restaurants or running convenience stores has only amplified their disappointment.

Foreigners hold less than 4 percent of formal jobs in South Africa, a rate that has remained mostly unchanged for more than a decade, according to an article published in June by researchers at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. One in five participants in the informal economy — which includes roadside vending — is a foreigner, the researchers said.

As many South Africans turn to the sector because of the high unemployment rate, competition has increased.

But a report by the World Bank in 2018 also found that immigrants tended to take more business risks than South African citizens and that immigrant workers generate jobs for South Africans.

A common refrain among anti-immigrant activists is that foreigners use taxpayer-funded resources, like public health clinics and schools, depriving South African citizens.

South Africa has a school-choice system, and the best public schools fill quickly. Many South Africans argue that immigrant children are taking those prime slots.

Data does not support that argument. Foreigners account for just 2 percent of students in public schools, according to government statistics.

Government officials have raised concerns over the years that foreigners place a significant strain on the budgets of public medical facilities.

A 2023 government report found that at one of the country’s largest medical facilities, Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital in Johannesburg, over 40 percent of the patients were foreign nationals.

The researchers at Witwatersrand found that financial mismanagement by the government had squeezed public services, leading to longer wait times at medical facilities and larger student-to-teacher ratios. Those pressures have the potential to increase anti-immigrant sentiment in the coming years, they wrote.

item.title: A Mother’s Crusade to Rid South Africa of African Immigrants
item.description:
On a clear morning last October, Nozie Khoza and her brigade of self-proclaimed patriots stood at the entrance of a public health clinic in Johannesburg on a quest to shape South Africa in their image.

When the gate opened at 7:30, the group demanded to see IDs from everyone seeking to enter, saying that only South Africans would be allowed inside.

“You belong to Nigeria, sweetheart,” Bongi Nomnganga, one of Ms. Khoza’s allies, told a young woman, turning her away because, even though she had a South African ID, her last name was Nigerian.

“It smells like fraud,” another one of Ms. Khoza’s associates said of a young woman’s South African ID, after the woman told them her parents were from Mozambique.

Ms. Khoza, a 39-year-old mother of two, had no authority to determine who could enter the public clinic.

Rather, she is a foot soldier in a highly organized network of activists going to extreme lengths to harass immigrants in South Africa, most of whom come from other African nations in search of opportunity in the continent’s largest economy.

Polls show a growing number of South Africans share hostility toward immigrants and want the government to do more to thwart the heavy flow of migrants entering the country. There have been nationwide protests and violence. Immigrants have been attacked and even killed, chased from their homes and businesses.

Despite a lack of evidence, many South Africans blame immigrants for crime, for stealing jobs and for taking up valuable public resources in a nation with high unemployment and growing inequality. They say they have lost faith in the government and have taken the law into their own hands.

This wave of anti-immigrant furor echoes movements seen in the United States and Europe. But only 5 percent of South Africa’s 65 million people are immigrants, according to government statistics.

Foreigners accounted for just 3 percent of arrests over the past five years, according to police data. They accounted for just 1.2 percent of arrests for violent crimes over the same period.

Still, officials have ramped up workplace inspections, punishing employers who hire undocumented foreigners. More than 53,000 foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated from South Africa since June, the government said last week.

Cyril Ramaphosa, the president, has announced new investments to secure the nation’s border, and he has repeatedly warned South Africans not to engage in vigilante justice.

But the police have not always intervened when citizens harass foreigners.

“It’s only South Africa that is experiencing such an influx of foreigners every day,” Ms. Khoza told those waiting outside the public health clinic in Rosettenville, a neighborhood in southern Johannesburg.

“The schools are full of your kids. Healthcare is full of you. Workplace is full of you. Restaurants full of you.”

“There’s going to be a war,” she said.

Ms. Khoza was born and raised in Durban, the epicenter of much of the recent anti-immigrant unrest in South Africa. But it wasn’t until she moved to Johannesburg at 23 to work as a television extra and in production that she developed her grim view of immigrants.

She said she watched as the city deteriorated over time and blamed the urban blight on immigrant street vendors. She blamed foreign landlords for not taking care of dilapidated properties.

A construction company she owns stopped getting business. She claims it was because Zimbabweans were underbidding her for contracts. She also says she had to send her daughter to private school because the public schools nearest her home were at capacity. She blamed this on immigrant children overcrowding the school system.

Ms. Khoza’s frustration led her to become an outspoken member of a national anti-immigrant group called March and March. The group targets all foreigners — not just those in the country illegally — and wants them gone.

On a Saturday in May, Ms. Khoza joined a group of about 50 people who marched down a residential street near her neighborhood. Their goal was to raid a home they said had been overrun by illegal Congolese immigrants.

They stopped at a house in the middle of the block to carry out what the group called an eviction. It did not matter that the Congolese family living inside was there legally.

The mob used bolt cutters to break through the driveway gate. They banged on the doors and jostled the burglar bars on the windows. The house was dark and seemed empty.

A few minutes later, the mob breached the front door. Teary-eyed children emerged from a dark corridor, hustling out of the house, shivering.

“We are sorry,” some of them squealed.

Their mother, Sandra, an immigrant from the Democratic Republic of Congo, shuffled out in shock as she cradled her youngest child in a blanket, a two-week-old baby. Tall with her hair braided in cornrows, Sandra’s eyes welled with tears as she confronted the angry crowd.

While all the banging was going on outside, Sandra, 38, had been hiding inside with seven of her eight children. She called her husband, Pierre, who was out at the time, and he went straight to a police station to report a break-in. (Both she and her husband asked that their last names be withheld for their safety.)

Having lived nearly half of her life in South Africa, Sandra knew how dangerous situations like this could be. In 2008, the year she arrived after fleeing civil war in Congo, South Africa experienced its first major spasm of xenophobic violence after apartheid, the era when many Black citizens were forced to flee the country’s violent white-led regime.

Vigilantes killed dozens of immigrants and destroyed many foreign-owned shops, leading tens of thousands of foreigners to flee the country. Violence spiked again in 2015 and 2019.

Other African nations have watched these waves of anti-immigrant violence in disbelief, shocked to see so many South Africans turn their backs on people from countries that provided refuge during apartheid. Nigeria has demanded that South Africa compensate its citizens who have been forced to leave their homes and businesses.

Over the years, Sandra, whose house was raided, had learned how to survive as a foreigner in South Africa. She knew not to answer her cellphone in a crowded taxi so no one would recognize her accent. She knew not to play Congolese music too loudly at home or in the hair salon she owned. She knew how to dress like a South African.

She and her husband said they always keep their immigration paperwork up to date and have legal status as asylum seekers. None of that seemed to matter to the angry mob shoving its way into her house.

The group stormed the family’s home and dumped their belongings on the street.

Pierre, 47, was incredulous when he arrived with the police. He had migrated from Congo in 2008 and met Sandra in Johannesburg. He tried to pacify the crowd by speaking Zulu to them and showing photos of a traditional Zulu wedding ceremony he had with a South African woman he called his second wife.

The mob still wanted them out.

Ms. Khoza has been watching with envy clips of U.S. immigration agents raiding American streets to capture and deport illegal immigrants under the Trump administration.

“The government here should be doing exactly what Trump is doing,” she said, “so that South Africa can have order and South Africans are put first.”

While they wait for the government to act, groups like March and March have asked organizers like Ms. Khoza to be as loud as possible and to make a scene wherever they go.

At Pierre’s house, neighbors flocked to the street to gawk. The block was jammed with police vehicles, a heap of furniture and the mob’s shouting.

Pierre called his landlord, Dermot Connors. When Mr. Connors arrived, he explained that Pierre and his family were lawful tenants and he begged the mob to let the children back inside.

They refused.

Mr. Connors asked the police to intervene, but a police captain told him he was concerned about a potential standoff. “I don’t want to promote violence,” the captain said, adding that the best solution was for the family to find somewhere else to stay for the night.

Sandra stood anguished over her family’s scattered belongings. The keyboard that their eldest child plays at church. The colored pencils that their younger children use for schoolwork. The framed certificate Pierre received from a former employer, praising his “commitment and dedication.”

As the invaders lounged on the family’s furniture, Sandra spotted a familiar face in the crowd. It was Ms. Khoza, whom Sandra said had blocked her several times from getting care at the public health clinic in Rosettenville.

Ms. Khoza later said she did not recognize Sandra but felt remorse about what Sandra’s children endured.

“I felt bad a bit,” she said. “I don’t want to lie.”

Ms. Khoza said the defense of her own children went hand-in-hand with her effort to rid South Africa of immigrants. Last year, she explained to her eldest daughter, Owethu, that foreign nationals were taking over their country.

“I am a victim,” Owethu, 17, said in an interview, adding that she sees her mother and others like her as being on a noble pursuit.

“I think they’re brave because they’re fighting against police, they’re fighting against the government,” she said.

That battle continued the day after a recent nationwide anti-immigrant protest on June 30. The organizers had given that date as a deadline for all undocumented migrants to leave the country, and Ms. Khoza hoped to see fewer immigrants on the streets of Johannesburg.

Instead, she saw many immigrant street vendors selling goods just as before.

“It’s no longer allowed to sell here,” Ms. Khoza told a man selling vegetables. “There are people coming here to check the situation. Pack quickly.”

“We told you to leave by yesterday and you are still here,” Ms. Nomnganga, her associate, chimed in.

As the women went from one stall to another, the vendors were rattled and hustled to pack their onions and cellphone cases and socks.

“I have papers,” one of the vendors said, holding up a plastic bag with her passport.

“Mama, we don’t want your permit,” Ms. Khoza said. “The only thing we want is only South Africans in our country.”

The woman packed up her goods and walked away.

item.title: Zelensky Dismisses Ukraine’s Top General After Protests
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine removed his top general on Tuesday night amid swelling public protests and growing concerns that the national unity that had helped the country survive nearly five years of war was in danger of fracturing.

The dismissal of the general, Oleksandr Syrskyi, was a major reversal for Mr. Zelensky, who just days earlier sided with him and fired Ukraine’s defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.

Mr. Zelensky said he was replacing General Syrskyi with Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, the commander of the Joint Forces. The choice was likely to please the protesters, after Mr. Drapatyi had publicly sided with Mr. Fedorov in his clash with General Syrskyi over warfighting strategy.

Thousands of people had joined mass demonstrations to pressure Mr. Zelensky to change course and reaffirm Mr. Fedorov’s vision of warfare as increasingly dominated by drones and robots. As he championed a military overhaul that leaned into high-tech innovation, Mr. Fedorov, 35, emerged as a symbol of hope to many Ukrainians, particularly young people.

General Drapatyi, 43, is part of a younger generation of Ukrainian officers. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, he built a reputation as a frontline commander focused on tactical innovation, drone integration and direct accountability. He is generally highly regarded by rank-and-file soldiers and military reformers alike.

Mr. Fedorov’s dismissal after only six months as defense minister came as Ukraine seemed to finally have regained the initiative in the war, in large part through the increasingly effective use of long- and medium-range drones to strike targets in Russia and Crimea.

Mr. Zelensky said that he had been forced to choose between Mr. Fedorov and General Syrskyi as the differences between their camps had become impossible to resolve.

Ultimately, as the protests grew, it became clear that the rift extended far beyond a clash of personalities. For many Ukrainians, Mr. Fedorov embodied a tech-driven path to victory that might spare lives, while General Syrskyi had come to represent the darkest, most punishing realities of a war fought through sheer attrition.

General Syrskyi, 60, played a crucial role in the defense of Kyiv early in the war and in a counteroffensive in Kharkiv in September 2022. He was appointed commander in chief of the armed forces in February 2024.

In a statement on Tuesday night, Mr. Zelensky praised the general for his service, saying that he had “delivered results” and that “every warrior deserves to be treated with dignity.”

Like many senior Ukrainian commanders, General Syrskyi was trained in the Soviet military system, where personal loyalty was frequently valued over tactical innovation. Critics described him as rigid and out of touch, and he never won widespread public admiration.

During the prolonged and bloody 2023 battle of Bakhmut, General Syrskyi earned the nickname “the Butcher” for his perceived tolerance of high casualties for limited tactical gains. It was a narrative he disputed, saying that preserving soldiers’ lives was his top priority.

Criticism of General Syrskyi erupted almost immediately after Mr. Fedorov was fired. Veterans, analysts and active-duty soldiers accused General Syrskyi of blocking initiatives to adapt to a rapidly changing battlefield. Protesters took to the streets with signs bearing variations of “Fedorov is innovation, old grandpas are degeneration.”

Mr. Fedorov said that the military establishment had resisted procurement reforms that he championed to promote competition and to sever informal ties between the General Staff and politically connected arms manufacturers.

He accused General Syrskyi of maneuvering behind the scenes to preserve his own power and said that instead of defeating Russia, the general had “figured out how to split the country.”

The situation reached a breaking point as dissent within the military spilled into the open.

Last week, General Drapatyi issued a rare public statement supporting Mr. Fedorov, writing, “Silence does not protect the army; it only allows mistakes to accumulate.”

Col. Pavlo Yelizarov, a deputy commander of the air force, submitted his resignation, calling Mr. Fedorov’s removal “a great blow to the country’s defense.”

Faced with this deepening turmoil, Mr. Zelensky met with brigade commanders to hear their concerns. His office urged patience at home while seeking to reassure allies abroad.

“The situation is being resolved professionally, constructively and in the interests of our state,” Kyrylo Budanov, the former intelligence chief who is now the head of the president’s office, said in a statement. “I ask everyone to remain calm.”

“The enemy is closely watching every one of our internal disagreements and is waiting for us to start fighting among ourselves,” he said. “To our enemies, I say this directly: You will not live to see it.”

Mr. Zelensky spent days huddled with senior military leaders from across the ranks and sought to bring Mr. Fedorov back into the fold.

After meeting with the president, Mr. Fedorov said a constructive dialogue to address his concerns had begun. “There will definitely be changes,” he said in a statement.

Since Ukrainians have largely accepted that there can be no elections while the war rages, mass demonstrations have become a pressure release valve and a check on power.

Last year, tens of thousands of Ukrainians staged protests across the country after an effort by Mr. Zelensky to neuter the nation’s anti-corruption agencies. The government quickly changed course in response to the protests.

The demonstrations that followed Mr. Fedorov’s firing exposed long-simmering tensions within the military. The infighting was profoundly dangerous, soldiers said, because it could undermine combat cohesion and worsen the military’s personnel crisis by driving disillusioned troops toward desertion.

General Syrskyi remained largely silent as the controversy swirled, posting only videos of himself meeting with commanders on the front. But on Monday, he published a column in the Militarnyi news outlet to respond to what he called a “mythology about conflicts” and to defend his tenure.

He wrote that he was surprised to learn of any conflict with Mr. Fedorov and apologized if any offense had been taken.

“Ukraine is bigger than Fedorov, Syrskyi and any of us,” he wrote. “Ukraine will stand not because it has irreplaceable people, but because it has an army, institutions and millions of people who do their job. Reducing this war to a confrontation between two people is the greatest service we can do to the enemy.”

Ultimately, Mr. Zelensky concluded that removing the general was the only way to restore unity.
